overview: The Aydınid Beylik was a Turkish principality in western Anatolia, conventionally founded around 1308 by Mehmed Bey. From Birgi, Ayasuluk, Tire, and İzmir, its rulers joined fertile inland valleys to Aegean ports. Umur Bey made it a major naval power, allied with Byzantine claimants, and fought a crusading coalition that captured lower Smyrna in 1344. Treaties connected merchants, grain, coin, and customs revenue with Venetian and Genoese networks. Mosques, baths, madrasas, books, translations, and medical writing reveal cultural patronage, while Ibn Battuta records hospitality, food, students, servants, and court ceremony. Bayezid I absorbed the beylik in 1390; Aydınid rule revived after Ankara in 1402 and ended definitively with Cüneyd Bey in 1426. The atlas instead paints the exact id only from 1400 to 1492. Its lone polygon appears during Ottoman occupation, extends decades beyond annexation, and folds much of neighboring Menteşe into Aydın. The card therefore uses a historical lifetime, names the interruption, and treats the shape as a faulty visual layer rather than a territorial fact.

periods.title: 1308 to 1310: Mehmed Bey establishes rule at Birgi
periods.summary: After fighting Sasa Bey, Mehmed Bey established an independent principality around Birgi about 1308. His forces consolidated nearby Tire and Ayasuluk while western Anatolia fragmented among competing powers. The early border remained a changing field of towns, valleys, fortresses, and loyalties rather than a fixed modern outline.

periods.title: 1310 to 1325: sons govern districts and ports grow
periods.summary: Mehmed Bey distributed districts among his sons while retaining senior authority. Birgi anchored the dynasty inland; Ayasuluk and İzmir connected it to the sea. Mosque building, tax collection, campaigning, and local negotiation helped turn conquest into government, although surviving narratives favor rulers over the households doing most daily work.

periods.title: 1325 to 1334: Umur builds naval power before succeeding
periods.summary: Umur commanded fleets from İzmir, raided and campaigned across the Aegean, and aided Byzantine allies. Ibn Battuta encountered both Umur and Mehmed in 1333, describing wealth, gifts, hospitality, and scholars. Mehmed died in 1334, after which his sons accepted Umur as the principal ruler.

periods.title: 1334 to 1344: Umur allies, campaigns, and faces a crusade
periods.summary: As ruler, Umur repeatedly supported John Kantakouzenos in Byzantine civil conflict and led forces through the Aegean and Balkans. His naval power alarmed Latin states and the papacy. In October 1344 a crusading fleet captured the lower harbor fortress of Smyrna, leaving the inland citadel under Aydınid control.

periods.title: 1344 to 1348: struggle for lower Smyrna ends with Umur death
periods.summary: Umur tried to recover lower Smyrna while continuing diplomacy and limited campaigning. Negotiations did not restore the port fortress. In 1348 he was killed during an assault on its defenses. His death ended the beylik's most expansive naval phase, and his elder brother Hızır assumed senior rule.

periods.title: 1348 to 1360: Hızır uses treaties after naval setbacks
periods.summary: Hızır governed after Umur and pursued agreements with Latin powers while the lower port of Smyrna remained outside Aydınid hands. Ayasuluk, Balat, and inland markets still supported exchange. The surviving treaties expose merchants, customs, and diplomacy more clearly than farm labor, household budgets, or ordinary travel.

periods.title: 1360 to 1390: Isa Bey sponsors learning and monumental building
periods.summary: Isa Bey's long rule brought prominent scholarly and architectural patronage at Ayasuluk and Birgi. The Isa Bey Mosque, medical and literary works, and book culture belong to this setting. In 1390 Bayezid I imposed Ottoman authority; Isa retained some charitable property but independent Aydınid rule stopped.

periods.title: 1390 to 1426: occupation, restoration, rivalry, and final conquest
periods.summary: Ottoman occupation lasted until Timur defeated Bayezid at Ankara in 1402 and restored Aydınid claimants. Cüneyd then fought relatives, rival princes, and successive Ottoman rulers, sometimes governing under their authority. Ottoman forces finally cornered him near the coast; he surrendered, and he and his family were killed in 1426.

sections.title: Identify the Aydınid beylik and challenge its map

items.text: The repository indexes exact id beylik-of-aydin as “Beylik of Aydin,” an approximate 1400 to 1492 state from historical basemaps. Coverage finds one border file and a missing review. No card or researched override yet distinguishes the Aydınid dynasty from later Ottoman Aydın or the modern place.

All fifty border snapshots were decoded. The exact id occurs only in world-1400, with properties from 1400 to 1492 and precision one. It is absent in 1279 and disappears by 1492, even though the historical beylik began around 1308 and ended in 1426.

The sole feature is one Polygon, one ring, and forty-five positions, bounded roughly by 26.390 to 30.696 east and 36.079 to 38.713 north. Tested Birgi, Ayasuluk, İzmir, Aydın, Tire, Kuşadası, and Balat fall inside, giving the shape a recognizable Aydınid core.

The same polygon also contains tested Milas, Bodrum, Muğla, Denizli, and Sardis, absorbing much Menteşe country and stretching beyond a defensible Aydınid core. Manisa, Bergama, Balıkesir, Kütahya, Bursa, Ankara, Konya, and Antalya remain outside. Valid geometry does not guarantee valid history.

At 1400, the atlas shows Aydınid sovereignty although Bayezid I had absorbed the beylik in 1390 and restoration followed only after Ankara in 1402. The exact layer also survives until 1492, sixty-six years after final annexation. Its only direct arc seam is Ottoman, with no positive-area overlap.

sections.title: Build a principality through towns, districts, war, and negotiation

items.text: Mehmed Bey emerged from Germiyan service and defeated Sasa Bey while securing Birgi and surrounding towns. Calling 1308 a foundation date is useful but approximate: conquest, allegiance, tax-taking, garrisoning, and dynastic recognition did not all begin on one morning. The card therefore marks the start as circa.

Mehmed assigned districts to sons, including Umur at İzmir and Ibrahim around Bodamya, while remaining senior ruler. This arrangement joined family government with local military responsibility. It also created later claims and rivalries. A dynastic family tree was simultaneously a map of offices, incomes, and possible quarrels.

Aydınid authority varied by town and moment. Birgi served as an early capital, Ayasuluk became a major court and market center, and upper İzmir remained important after crusaders seized the lower harbor fortress. Ports, citadels, valleys, roads, and agreements mattered more than a clean continuous frontier.

War included cavalry movement, fortress defense, raiding, sieges, shipbuilding, and service abroad. Umur also intervened in Byzantine civil conflict as an ally, not simply as a permanent enemy. Such coalitions changed quickly and exposed soldiers, sailors, captives, carriers, and residents to risks that victory stories compress.

After 1402, restoration did not return a calm earlier order. Cüneyd competed with relatives, attached himself to Ottoman succession struggles, bargained with Byzantines and Latins, and changed alignments. His career shows a small polity navigating larger contests, but frequent allegiance did not make Aydın identical with any temporary patron.

sections.title: Sail, trade, mint, and keep maritime claims in proportion

items.text: Umur organized fleets containing galleys and smaller vessels, moved troops across the Aegean, and became a consequential ally in Byzantine warfare. Ships required timber, rope, sails, metalwork, food, water, rowers, sailors, pilots, and shore labor. Chronicles praise commanders while leaving most of that supply chain anonymous.

Raids reached islands and Balkan coasts, but an itinerary of attack is not a property deed. The audited polygon correctly leaves Chios, Samos, Rhodes, and Lesbos outside. Naval reach, tribute, temporary landing, alliance, commerce, piracy, and territorial government must remain separate claims rather than one blue patch.

Agreements with Venice regulated peace, merchants, consuls, customs, and movement at ports including Ayasuluk and Balat. Grain and other goods linked inland producers with maritime buyers. Treaty clauses describe intended privileges; they do not prove that every merchant traveled safely, paid the same rate, or won every dispute.

Genoese and other Latin merchants also negotiated within a competitive Aegean economy. Political hostility and trade could coexist because rulers needed revenue and buyers needed supplies. Merchants still faced seizure, changing alliances, storms, credit risk, and local tolls. A signed treaty was useful equipment, not favorable weather.

A coin hoard from Ayasuluk includes imported Italian silver, evidence of monetary connections by the early fourteenth century. Later Aydınid issues and a bath hoard show local minting and saving. Coins illuminate metal, authority, and circulation, but not every price, wage, debt, barter exchange, or household budget.

sections.title: Farm, cook, make, carry, and encounter unequal consumption

items.text: The Büyük and Küçük Menderes valleys supported grain, orchards, vines, gardens, livestock, and movement between inland settlements and ports. Producers faced seasonal labor, water variation, transport costs, taxes, and warfare. Commercial grain exports show surplus in some places and years, not permanent abundance in every kitchen.

Ibn Battuta's Birgi host supplied assorted fruit, prepared food, lodging, and fodder for the visitors' animals during summer heat. This is unusually vivid evidence for hospitality and provisioning. It records a successful welcome, not a census of ordinary diets, meal frequency, scarcity, or who cooked and cleaned.

Mosques, baths, fortifications, houses, ships, manuscripts, textiles, tools, and pottery required quarrying, carpentry, carving, firing, weaving, tanning, metalworking, hauling, and repair. Birgi's buildings preserve several materials and inherited techniques. Finished monuments survive more readily than the sore hands, workshops, and discarded practice pieces behind them.

Ayasuluk's court could serve sherbet, biscuits, and meals with elaborate presentation, while servants and enslaved attendants performed visible work. Court consumption reveals access to goods and ceremony at the top. It cannot establish what rural laborers ate, whether children received equal portions, or how families managed shortage.

Markets connected peasants, fishers, herders, carriers, brokers, craftspeople, money changers, tax collectors, resident traders, and visitors speaking several languages. The sources identify ports and agreements more easily than bargaining voices. A customs clause could count sacks; it rarely recorded who mended the sack first.

sections.title: Meet households, women, children, dependents, and religious communities

items.text: Aydınid political history exposes elite fathers, sons, brothers, daughters, marriages, and dependents because succession turned kinship into public conflict. Ordinary households remain much less visible. They likely combined care, production, worship, inheritance, and mutual aid in varied forms, but no source supports one universal Aydınid family model.

Mehmed's sons received territories, and later rulers used marriage to create alliances or settle claims. Dynastic women are seldom described on their own terms. Silence about their choices, property management, childbirth, care work, or political mediation reflects the records, not proof that such activity was absent.

Ibn Battuta names students, a professor, servants, and enslaved people around Birgi's learned and courtly households. Greek captives also entered service after warfare and raiding. Their presence reveals coercive inequality as well as cultural contact; a gifted person was not a cheerful souvenir, however casually a traveler recorded it.

Ahi lodges offered travelers food, shelter, company, and urban connections. Mosques, madrasas, tombs, lodges, and rural teachers structured religious life beyond court ceremony. Participation varied by place, gender, status, and community, and the survival of Muslim institutions does not erase Christian residents or other local traditions.

Children learned speech, manners, belief, household tasks, farming, herding, craft, and market behavior through relatives and experienced workers. Elite sons might train for command or administration. No Aydınid child register records starting ages, games, discipline, mortality, disability, or girls' instruction, so specific childhood routines remain uncertain.

sections.title: Learn in madrasas, workshops, courts, and books

items.text: Ibn Battuta met the Birgi madrasa professor Muhyiddin and learned that his local host was also a student. The episode securely shows a teacher, pupils, status, translation, and hospitality. It does not supply enrollment totals, a daily timetable, admission rules, examinations, fees, or equal access across society.

Madrasas taught advanced religious and legal learning to selected students, while mosques and lodges supported other instruction. Birgi's surviving and documented educational buildings show patronage, not a universal school network. Children and apprentices also learned outside classrooms, where practice rarely generated the tidy paperwork historians would appreciate.

At court, Muhyiddin translated Arabic prophetic reports into Turkish for Mehmed Bey. Such moments show multilingual mediation among Arabic scholarship, Persianate literary culture, and spoken or written Turkish. They do not establish mass literacy. Interpretation could matter as much as reading when rulers, visitors, clerks, and audiences lacked a shared language.

Kul Mesud prepared an Old Anatolian Turkish version of Kalila wa Dimna for Umur Bey, adapting a widely traveled book of animal fables and political advice. Patronage helped vernacular prose grow. One commissioned translation still tells us more about courtly literary ambition than about what most households read.

Aydınid patrons supported scholars, poets, physicians, copyists, illuminators, binders, and artisans. Manuscript research shows that books were designed objects as well as texts. Preparing paper, ink, pigments, layout, script, and binding required coordinated skill; even a medical manuscript needed more than a physician with excellent handwriting.

sections.title: Treat sickness, write medicine, and bound claims about care

items.text: Hacı Paşa studied medicine in Cairo, returned to Aydınid territory, and served Isa Bey as physician, judge, and teacher at Ayasuluk or Birgi. His career links learned medicine with law and education. It documents an exceptional practitioner near court, not a physician available equally to every village household.

Hacı Paşa wrote Shifa al-asqam and other medical works discussing diagnosis, regimen, drugs, and treatments. His writing drew on Islamicate learned medicine and practical observation. A book can reveal recommended care without showing how often advice was followed, which remedies families could afford, or how patients judged results.

A late fourteenth-century Aydınid medical manuscript preserves evidence of copying, illustration, and the circulation of health knowledge. Its survival is valuable precisely because routine care left little documentation. Manuscripts reached limited readers; household remedies, midwifery, nursing, trauma care, and local healers remain much harder to identify.

Court evidence mentions a Jewish physician honored by Mehmed Bey, while Hacı Paşa later worked for Isa. These cases show that rulers could seek expertise across communal boundaries. They do not justify a claim of uniform tolerance, a public medical service, or identical treatment for elites, soldiers, captives, women, and children.

No reviewed source identifies an Aydınid hospital, patient register, pharmacy network, vaccination practice, or public health office. Families, neighbors, religious figures, and practitioners likely provided care, but their exact roles are not documented. The card names learned medicine and the local institutional gap instead of importing Cairo's facilities.

sections.title: Find water, baths, heating, and the limits of sanitation evidence

items.text: Ayasuluk's Isa Bey bath included sequences of changing, warm, and hot spaces supported by reservoirs, furnaces, channels, and labor. Archaeology clarifies construction and heating better than admission, price, gender schedule, or frequency of use. A surviving bath is infrastructure evidence, not everyone's weekly calendar.

The UNESCO dossier places the bath, mosque, citadel, and other remains within a layered Ayasuluk settlement. Water had to be obtained, stored, heated, carried, and drained for worship, bathing, cooking, animals, and craft. Those tasks depended on workers and maintenance, not architecture operating by itself.

Government inventories preserve several historic baths across the region, but dates and later rebuilding differ. Baths supported washing, sociability, and employment while consuming fuel and water. Their presence does not prove universal access, constant operation, or that every resident understood cleanliness, privacy, and health in the same way.

Mosque courtyards and fountains could support ablution, while houses relied on more varied local arrangements. Reviewed evidence does not establish a citywide piped supply for Aydınid Birgi, Ayasuluk, or İzmir. Reservoirs and channels at a monumental complex should not be projected automatically into every lane or kitchen.

No reviewed source documents standard Aydınid toilets, household latrines, sewers, refuse collection, street-cleaning schedules, or disposal of human and animal waste. Such materials certainly required handling, but the methods remain unknown. A bath drain moved water; it did not secretly certify a municipal sanitation department.

sections.title: Recognize architecture, books, medicine, and secure writing

items.text: Birgi's Great Mosque, ordered by Mehmed Bey in 1312, joined worship with a madrasa, tomb, bath, carved wood, reused stone, and skilled construction. Its minbar is a celebrated work of woodworking. Attribution to a patron should not hide the designers, carvers, masons, carriers, donors, and maintainers.

Secure writing sample: original Arabic in Arabic script, “فتح هذه البلدة بنصر الله وتأييده”; transliteration “fataha hadhihi al-baldah bi-nasr Allahi wa-ta'yidihi”; translation “He conquered this town with God's victory and support.” It appears in Birgi Great Mosque's east portal inscription naming Mehmed bin Aydın, conquest in AH 707, and construction in AH 712.

The published corpus identifies the monumental lettering as Seljuk thuluth but does not securely name this inscription's composer or carver. That absence belongs with the sample. The quoted words advertise conquest and divine aid; they are a patronal public claim, not a transcript of how every resident described 1308.

Isa Bey commissioned the great mosque at Ayasuluk in 1375 from Ali of Damascus. Reused ancient columns, carved stone, tile, a courtyard, and a broad prayer hall joined local resources with wider Mediterranean design knowledge. The building demonstrates exchange among patrons and specialists more securely than any single cultural label.

Aydınid achievement also included naval organization, negotiated trade, vernacular translation, medical authorship, manuscript production, and urban patronage. None belonged to rulers alone. Sailors, farmers, merchants, interpreters, teachers, patients, copyists, builders, servants, and enslaved people made the polity function, although many survive only at the edge of elite records.

sections.title: End rule in 1426 and follow people beyond annexation

items.text: Bayezid I absorbed Aydın in 1390, leaving Isa Bey some control of charitable foundations while ending independent government. This was a real first termination, not merely a diplomatic pause. The historical lifetime spans it only to teach the dynasty's later restoration, and the period text marks sovereignty as suspended.

After Ankara in 1402, Timur restored Aydınid claimants, but Cüneyd soon dominated a fractured revival. His shifting ties to Ottoman princes, Byzantium, Venice, and neighboring beys kept the region in conflict. Restoration renewed dynastic rule without erasing twelve years of Ottoman administration or recreating an unchanged 1390 state.

In 1426 Ottoman forces and Genoese allies isolated Cüneyd near the coast. He surrendered after promised safety, then he and members of his family were killed. The conquest ended a credible independent Aydınid succession. The violence also makes “annexation” a household event, not only a color change.

Residents continued farming, trading, sailing, worshipping, bathing, learning, building, healing, marrying, and caring under Ottoman rule. Towns, routes, monuments, and skills crossed 1426 unevenly. Political continuity ended; human and material continuities did not. Later Aydın administration reused the dynastic name without becoming the same polity.

The Aydınid Beylik must remain separate from Germiyan service before foundation, Byzantine towns it conquered, Menteşe and Saruhan neighbors, the Ottoman occupation, the restored dynasty, and the later Ottoman province. The atlas conflates territory and chronology; the researched card corrects lifetime while refusing unsafe automated predecessor or successor links.

ending.text: In 1426, Ottoman forces supported at sea by Genoese allies cornered Cüneyd Bey near the Aegean coast. After he surrendered, Cüneyd and members of his family were killed, ending a credible independent Aydınid succession. This was the dynasty's final political termination after the earlier Ottoman absorption of 1390 and restoration following Ankara in 1402. Ottoman government continued in the region, and the name Aydın later survived in administrative and modern geography, but neither continuity makes the province or city the same state. Farmers, sailors, merchants, craftspeople, worshippers, teachers, physicians, patients, children, servants, and families remained, adapting across conquest while monuments and routes were reused. The atlas reverses the central chronology: it first paints exact id beylik-of-aydin in 1400, during Ottoman occupation, and leaves the feature active until 1492, sixty-six years after final annexation. The researched card therefore uses circa 1308 to 1426, explains the interruption, and records no automatic predecessor or successor association.
